3320: A short psalm in which David remembers being the youngest shepherd brother, chosen and anointed by God, and defeating Goliath. It sits at the end of the Greek, Syriac and Ethiopian Psalters, and a Hebrew form was found in the Dead Sea Scrolls. Orthodox and Ethiopians read it; Jews, Catholics and Protestants do not.
3321: David the youngest, shepherding his father's sheep
3322: His hands make an instrument; he gives glory to God
3323: God sends his messenger and anoints him above his brothers
3324: He kills the Philistine giant with his own sword and removes Israel's shame
3325:
Jews: the Masoretic Psalter has 150 psalms; this one was outside it (as even the Greek title concedes).

Catholics: it was not in Jerome's Latin Psalters as a canonical psalm and was not considered at Trent, so it never entered the Catholic canon (status n/a).

Protestants: outside both the Hebrew Bible and the Latin Apocrypha, so it was not even part of the Apocrypha debate.
3326:
Psalm 151 is in the Septuagint Psalter in major codices (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus) and so is read in Orthodox Bibles. The Syriac Psalter includes it with Psalms 152-155, and the Ethiopian Psalter includes it. The Qumran discovery shows it had a genuine Hebrew pre-history, which raised its standing among scholars.

It is valued as a meditation on God choosing the small and overlooked, a theme close to the heart of the Bible.
3327: Old Testament-era psalm; apostolicity does not apply.
3328: Hebrew text attested at Qumran; probably composed in the Second Temple period.
3329: Simply retells biblical events in praise of God.
3330: Read in the Greek, Syriac and Ethiopian Psalters; absent from Hebrew and Latin.
3331: Present in Eastern Psalters, though rarely prominent in liturgy.
3332: Attributed to David, but explicitly marked as outside the number.
3333: Mentions Psalm 151 as a psalm for those who are small and chosen.
3335: Published the Qumran Psalms Scroll containing the Hebrew Psalm 151.
3336: David, the youngest keeping the sheep, is anointed by Samuel in preference to his brothers.
3337: David the skilled player of the lyre.
3338: David kills Goliath and cuts off his head with the giant's own sword.
3339: God chooses the weak and lowly, the theme the psalm celebrates.
3348: Astronomical Book and Book of Watchers (oldest parts)
3351: Aramaic original (eleven fragmentary manuscripts at Qumran cover every section except the Parables); survives complete only in Ge'ez (classical Ethiopic), with Greek portions.
3352: A collection of five Jewish works written between about 300 BC and the turn of the era, in the land of Israel, attributed to Enoch, who walked with God (Gen 5:24).
3353:
1 Enoch is really a small library of five books. The Book of Watchers (ch. 1-36) expands Genesis 6:1-4: angels called Watchers, led by Shemihazah and Asael, descend, marry women, teach forbidden arts, and father giants whose violence brings the Flood; Enoch tours heaven, the places of punishment and the ends of the earth. The Parables or Similitudes (37-71) describe a heavenly figure called the Son of Man, the Chosen One and the Messiah, who will sit on the throne of glory and judge kings. The Astronomical Book (72-82) sets out a 364-day solar calendar. The Dream Visions (83-90) include the Animal Apocalypse, retelling Israel's history with animals for people up to the Maccabean revolt. The Epistle of Enoch (91-108) warns the rich and promises reward to the righteous.

Enoch was widely read by Jews before AD 70 and by early Christians. The New Testament letter of Jude quotes it directly (Jude 14-15 = 1 Enoch 1:9), and 1-2 Peter seem to know its story of imprisoned angels. Lost to the West for centuries, it was brought to Europe from Ethiopia by James Bruce in 1773 and first translated into English by Richard Laurence in 1821.
3354: An ancient Jewish collection written in Enoch's name, telling how rebel angels corrupted the world before the Flood, describing heaven, a coming judge called the Son of Man, and the end of evil. The New Testament letter of Jude quotes it. It is Scripture only in the Ethiopian Orthodox Church.
3355: Book of Watchers: fall of the angels, the giants, Enoch's heavenly journeys (ch. 1-36)
3356: Parables: the Son of Man and the judgement of kings (ch. 37-71)
3358: Dream Visions: the Animal Apocalypse of Israel's history (ch. 83-90)
3359: Epistle of Enoch and Apocalypse of Weeks (ch. 91-108)
3360:
Jews: although Enoch was popular at Qumran and in Second Temple Judaism, rabbinic Judaism did not receive it; it was attributed to a pre-Flood figure (so it could not have been written down and preserved through the Flood, as some argued), it promoted a solar calendar against the Temple's lunar one, and its angel-centred apocalyptic world fell out of favour after AD 70.

Christians (Catholic, Protestant, Orthodox): after early enthusiasm, the Fathers doubted it. Augustine said it could not be proved genuine because of its extreme antiquity and that the Jews did not accept it, so it should not be trusted even if it contained some truth. Jerome reported it was counted among the apocrypha. Its angel-marriage story was rejected by those who read Genesis 6 of Seth's line. That Jude quotes it was taken to mean only that Jude used a true saying, as Paul quoted Greek poets (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12).
3361:
The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church received 1 Enoch with its Bible from earliest times and has preserved the only complete text. For them, Jude's quotation of Enoch as one who prophesied confirms its standing, as did its use by early Fathers.

Early Christians valued it: the Epistle of Barnabas cites Enoch as Scripture, and Tertullian argued it should be accepted, noting that Jude quotes it. Today scholars of every tradition value it as essential background to the New Testament: its Son of Man, its picture of fallen angels bound until judgement, Gehenna, and the coming judgement all shed light on Jesus' teaching and the apostles' letters.
3362: Not apostolic; attributed to Enoch, seventh from Adam, which nearly all scholars regard as pseudonymous.
3363: Parts are older than Daniel (3rd century BC), but far later than Enoch's claimed era.
3364: Its monotheism and judgement themes are orthodox; its angel-marriages, calendar and cosmology are disputed.
3365: Accepted as Scripture only in the Ethiopian church after the 4th century.
3366: Used by Barnabas, Tertullian and others early on; abandoned later except in Ethiopia.
3367: Presents itself throughout as revealed visions given to Enoch.
3368: Quotes Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesying that the Lord comes with his holy myriads to judge the ungodly (1 Enoch 1:9).
3370: Cites Enoch with an introduction normally used for Scripture.
3371: Defends Enoch's authority, arguing the Jews rejected it because it speaks of Christ and noting that Jude quotes it.
3372: Grants Enoch wrote some divine things but says the books under his name are excluded because their origin cannot be verified and the Jews did not keep them.
3374: Made the first English translation from Ethiopic manuscripts brought to Europe by James Bruce.
3375: A direct quotation of 1 Enoch 1:9, introduced as Enoch's prophecy.
3376: Angels who left their proper home, kept in chains in darkness until judgement, matches the Watchers story (1 Enoch 10).
3377: God cast sinning angels into Tartarus in chains of darkness; close to 1 Enoch 10 and 20.
3378: Christ's proclamation to the spirits in prison from Noah's time is often read against Enoch's imprisoned Watchers.
3379: The sons of God and daughters of men, the brief text the Book of Watchers expands.
3380: Enoch walked with God and was not, the basis for traditions of his heavenly knowledge.
3381: The Son of Man sitting on his glorious throne to judge resembles the Parables of Enoch (1 Enoch 62).
3392: Apocalypse of Moses (in some ancient references)
3393: Hebrew original (about fifteen copies at Qumran); survives complete only in Ge'ez, with Latin, Greek and Syriac fragments.
3394: A priestly Jewish author in Judea in the mid-2nd century BC, close to the circles that produced the Qumran community.
3395:
Jubilees retells Genesis 1 to Exodus 12 (and the Sinai setting of Exodus 24) as a revelation given to Moses on Mount Sinai by an angel of the presence, who dictates from heavenly tablets. History is organised into periods of 49 years (jubilees), and the whole runs fifty jubilees from creation to the entry into Canaan.

The author fills gaps (names of Adam's daughters and Noah's wives, Abraham rejecting his father's idols), smooths moral difficulties, and above all shows that the patriarchs already kept the Law: Sabbath, festivals, purity and a 364-day solar calendar that he insists on against a lunar one. He forbids intermarriage and nakedness (a reaction to Greek gymnasium culture), and gives a strong role to angels and to Mastema, chief of evil spirits. The Qumran Damascus Document refers to it as an authority.
3396: A retelling of Genesis and early Exodus, presented as what an angel revealed to Moses on Mount Sinai, showing the patriarchs already keeping the Law and a 364-day calendar. It was popular at Qumran. Only the Ethiopian Orthodox Church counts it as Scripture.
3397: Prologue: Moses on Sinai receives the history from the angel of the presence (ch. 1)
3399: Adam to Noah; the Watchers and the Flood (ch. 3-10)
3400: Abraham's rejection of idols and his covenant life (ch. 11-23)
3402: Moses, the Exodus and the Passover; Sabbath laws (ch. 46-50)
3403:
Jews: rabbinic Judaism followed the lunar calendar Jubilees condemns, and it did not accept a second Sinai revelation alongside the Torah. Its sectarian flavour (shared with Qumran) made it unacceptable to mainstream post-70 Judaism.

Christians: never part of the Greek or Latin Bibles; Fathers such as Epiphanius and Jerome knew it as an apocryphal Little Genesis. Its claim to be dictated to Moses and its legal rigour made it of limited Christian interest outside Ethiopia.
3404:
The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church received it as canonical Scripture and preserved its only complete text. Ethiopian readers value its strong Sabbath and festival theology and its harmony with their Enoch tradition and calendar concerns.

Scholars of all traditions value it as one of the most important examples of rewritten Bible, revealing how Jews around 150 BC read Genesis and the debates over calendar, Law and Gentile culture that shaped the Judaism of Jesus' day.
3405: Not apostolic; presented as Mosaic but generally regarded as pseudonymous.
3406: Mid-2nd century BC, contemporary with Daniel in many datings.
3407: Monotheistic and Torah-centred; its calendar and Law-before-Sinai claims are distinctive.
3408: Canonical only in Ethiopia; important at Qumran.
3409: Read at Qumran and in Ethiopia; little use elsewhere.
3410: Claims dictation by an angel from heavenly tablets to Moses.
3412: Refers readers to the book of the divisions of the times into their jubilees and weeks as an authority.
3414: Refers to Jubilees, also called Little Genesis, for details such as names of Adam's children.
3415: Mentions the apocryphal book Little Genesis in discussing place names.
3416: Moses forty days on the mountain, the setting for the whole revelation in Jubilees.
3417: The Law ordained through angels, an idea Jubilees dramatises with the angel of the presence.
3418: Stephen speaks of the Law received as delivered by angels.
3419: Creation and the Sabbath, which Jubilees retells with the angels' Sabbath-keeping.
3420: Terah served other gods; Jubilees expands this into Abraham's rejection of idols.
3429: Testament of Reuben, Simeon, Levi ... Benjamin
3430: Christian composition using Jewish sources (de Jonge)
3431: Jewish core with Christian interpolations (Charles, Kee)
3432: Greek as we have it; Jewish sources in Aramaic and Hebrew lie behind parts (the Aramaic Levi Document and a Hebrew Naphtali text were found at Qumran).
3433: Disputed: either a Jewish work of the 2nd-1st century BC later edited by Christians, or a Christian composition of the late 2nd century AD drawing on Jewish traditions. Either way the present form is Christian.
3434:
Modelled on Jacob's blessing of his sons (Gen 49), this work gives the deathbed speech of each of Jacob's twelve sons. Each patriarch tells his life story, confesses a besetting sin or celebrates a virtue, gives moral teaching, and predicts the future of his tribe. Reuben warns against sexual sin (recalling Bilhah), Simeon against envy, Judah against drunkenness and greed, Joseph praises chastity (Potiphar's wife) and brotherly love, Issachar commends simplicity.

Two recurring ideas stand out: love for God and for one's neighbour as the summary of the Law (strikingly close to Jesus' double commandment), and a coming salvation from the tribes of Levi and Judah, priest and king. Several passages plainly speak of God becoming man and of the Gentiles' salvation, which shows Christian hands. Robert Grosseteste's Latin translation (1242) made it popular in medieval Europe.
3435: The farewell speeches of Jacob's twelve sons, each warning against a sin or praising a virtue and predicting the future. It contains strikingly Christian-sounding lines, because Christians edited or wrote it. It is not Scripture in any major church, though it was popular in the Armenian church and the Middle Ages.
3436: Frame: each son gathers his children before death (modelled on Gen 49)
3437: Life story and confession: Reuben (lust), Simeon (envy), Judah (greed and drink), Gad (hatred)
3438: Virtues: Joseph (chastity and forgiveness), Issachar (simplicity), Zebulun (compassion), Benjamin (a good mind)
3439: Levi's heavenly ascent and the new priest (Testament of Levi 2-5, 18)
3440: Love of God and neighbour as the heart of the Law
3441: Future salvation through Levi and Judah, with Christian passages on God appearing as man
3442: No major Jewish or Christian body ever listed it among its Scriptures. Jews did not transmit it (only some Aramaic and Hebrew sources survived at Qumran). For Christians it was a late, pseudonymous edifying book; Origen mentions it with caution. The Armenian Bible tradition sometimes included it, but that church is outside the six traditions here.
3443: It was read widely as moral teaching: medieval Christians treasured it as an ancient Jewish witness to Christ, and Grosseteste believed the Jews had hidden it because of its prophecies. Modern scholars value it for the Jewish ethics it preserves (on sexuality, envy, anger and love of neighbour) and for the debate it raises about how Jewish texts were Christianised.
3444: Not apostolic; attributed to Jacob's sons.
3445: Possibly 2nd-1st century BC in its Jewish core; Christian form 2nd century AD.
3446: Its ethics are orthodox; its eschatology mixes Jewish and Christian ideas.
3447: Never received as Scripture by any major church; Armenian use is partial.
3448: Read devotionally, especially in the medieval West and Armenia.
3449: Presents prophecies from the patriarchs, but as testaments rather than claimed Scripture.
3450: Mentions a book called the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs in a homily, as a writing not in the canon.
3452: Translated it into Latin from a Greek manuscript, spreading it in medieval Europe.
3453: Jacob's blessing of his twelve sons is the model for the testaments.
3454: Jesus' double commandment closely resembles the Testaments' repeated call to love the Lord and your neighbour (Testament of Issachar 5:2; Testament of Dan 5:3).
3455: Joseph resisting Potiphar's wife, central to the Testament of Joseph.
3456: Reuben's sin with Bilhah, the confession at the heart of the Testament of Reuben.
3457: A priest of a new order; the Testament of Levi 18 speaks of a new priest raised up by God.
3465: Earliest psalms (after Pompey's capture of Jerusalem)
3467: Hebrew original (lost); survives in Greek and Syriac.
3468: Pious Jews in Jerusalem, often linked with Pharisaic circles (debated), reacting to the Roman general Pompey's capture of Jerusalem in 63 BC and the failures of the Hasmonean rulers.
3469:
These eighteen psalms, attributed to Solomon, lament the Roman conquest of Jerusalem. They describe a foreign conqueror (clearly Pompey) breaching the walls, entering the sanctuary, and later being killed on the shores of Egypt, and they blame the disaster on the sins of Jerusalem's own leaders who usurped David's throne (the Hasmoneans). The righteous accept God's discipline; the sinners will perish.

Psalms 17 and 18 contain the fullest pre-Christian portrait of the Davidic Messiah: a son of David who will purge Jerusalem of Gentiles and sinners, shepherd the people in righteousness, smash the arrogant like a potter's jar with an iron rod, destroy enemies by the word of his mouth, and be called the Lord Messiah. They are crucial for understanding what many Jews hoped for when Jesus was hailed as Son of David.
3470: Eighteen psalms written after the Romans captured Jerusalem in 63 BC, mourning the city and hoping for a righteous Son of David, the Messiah. They show what many Jews expected of the Messiah in Jesus' time. No major church counts them as Scripture.
3471: Lament over Jerusalem's sins and the Roman invasion (Pss. 1-2, 8)
3472: The righteous and the sinners contrasted (Pss. 3-4, 13-15)
3474: Pompey's death in Egypt seen as judgement (Ps. 2)
3475: The coming Son of David, the Lord Messiah (Ps. 17)
3476: Blessing on the generation of the Messiah (Ps. 18)
3477: Jews did not transmit them, and they were attributed to Solomon only artificially. In the Greek Christian world they were sometimes copied with the Bible: the table of contents of Codex Alexandrinus lists them after the New Testament with 1-2 Clement, and the Stichometry of Nicephorus lists them among disputed books (antilegomena). They never became canonical, hence rejected (in the sense of disputed and not received) for the Greek tradition, and n/a elsewhere.
3478: Some Syriac Bible manuscripts transmit them alongside the Odes of Solomon. Scholars value them highly as a dated witness (63-48 BC) to Jewish piety and messianic hope just before Jesus, to the idea of the righteous suffering discipline, and to the Pharisee-era debates about the Temple and the Hasmoneans.
3479: Not apostolic; attributed to Solomon pseudonymously.
3480: Mid-1st century BC, after the Jewish prophetic period.
3481: Classic Jewish psalmody and messianic hope.
3482: Known in some Greek and Syriac manuscripts but never broadly received.
3483: Little evidence of public reading in churches.
3484: Psalms ascribed to Solomon; no explicit prophetic claim.
3485: Its table of contents lists the Psalms of Solomon after the New Testament and 1-2 Clement (the pages are lost).
3487: Lists the Psalms and Odes of Solomon among the disputed Old Testament books.
3488: The angel announces a Saviour who is Christ the Lord, the same title (Lord Messiah) as Psalms of Solomon 17:32.
3489: Breaking the nations with a rod of iron like a potter's vessel, which Psalms of Solomon 17:23-24 applies to the Son of David.
3490: The rod of iron image applied to the victorious Christ.
3491: Striking the earth with the rod of his mouth, echoed in Psalms of Solomon 17:24.
3492: Crowds hail Jesus as Son of David, a title Psalms of Solomon 17 shows was loaded with messianic hope.
3503: Probably Hebrew original, then Greek (a few Greek fragments survive); complete only in one Syriac manuscript (the 6th-7th century Codex Ambrosianus in Milan); the closing letter circulated separately in many Syriac Bibles.
3504: A Jewish author in the land of Israel writing a generation after the Roman destruction of the Temple in AD 70, using the Babylonian destruction as a mask.
3505:
2 Baruch is a twin of 4 Ezra, written in the same years and wrestling with the same catastrophe. Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, sees angels dismantle Jerusalem's walls and hide the Temple vessels before the Babylonians enter, so that the enemy cannot boast. He laments, fasts and receives visions: a period of twelve woes, then the Messiah's revelation, when Behemoth and Leviathan will be food for the righteous and the earth will yield ten-thousandfold; the resurrection, in which the dead rise in their old form to be recognised and then are transformed; and a vision of dark and bright waters summarising history.

Unlike 4 Ezra, Baruch is more confident: the Law remains, and Israel must keep it. He ends with a letter to the nine and a half tribes in exile urging faithfulness. A famous line insists on personal responsibility: Adam is the cause only for himself; each of us has become our own Adam.
3506: A Jewish book written about AD 100 after Rome destroyed the Temple, in which Jeremiah's scribe Baruch mourns, receives visions of the Messiah and the resurrection, and urges Israel to keep the Law. Only one complete copy survives, in Syriac. No church counts it as Scripture, though its closing letter was copied in Syriac Bibles.
3507: Angels destroy Jerusalem before the enemy can (ch. 1-8)
3508: Laments and dialogues on why the righteous suffer (ch. 9-34)
3509: The twelve woes and the Messiah's age of plenty (ch. 25-30)
3511: Vision of the twelve dark and bright waters (ch. 53-74)
3512: Address to the people; letter to the exiled tribes (ch. 77-87)
3513: Jews: preserved only by Christians; rabbinic Judaism did not keep apocalypses. Christians: almost unknown in Greek and Latin, so it was never a candidate for the Western or Byzantine canons; its pseudonymous attribution and late date would have ruled it out in any case.
3514: In the Syriac church the Letter of Baruch (chapters 78-87) was copied in Bible manuscripts as a biblical book, and the whole apocalypse is in the great Milan Peshitta codex alongside 4 Ezra and 4 Maccabees. Scholars value it for Jewish beliefs about the resurrection body, the Messiah, the Law and human responsibility in the era when the Gospels and Paul's letters were being read.
3515: Not apostolic; attributed to Baruch pseudonymously.
3517: Jewish orthodoxy; its millennial abundance and resurrection teaching resemble early Christian views.
3519: The Letter of Baruch was read in the Syriac church.
3520: Presents itself as visions and divine speech to Baruch.
3522: The only complete manuscript, a Syriac Old Testament that includes 2 Baruch with 4 Ezra and 4 Maccabees.
3524: First published the Syriac text and a Latin translation.
3525: Baruch the scribe of Jeremiah, in whose name the book is written.
3526: Paul's death through Adam can be compared with 2 Baruch 54:15-19, which insists each person becomes his own Adam.
3527: Paul on what kind of body the dead are raised with parallels 2 Baruch 49-51.
3528: Behemoth, who in 2 Baruch 29 becomes food in the messianic age.
3529: A messianic reign before the final age, an idea 2 Baruch shares.
3537: Original composition in the Maccabean crisis, updated later
3538: Final form after Herod's death (4 BC)
3540: Hebrew or Aramaic original (lost), then Greek (lost); survives in one incomplete 6th-century Latin palimpsest found in Milan and published by Antonio Ceriani in 1861.
3541: A Jewish author in Judea in the early 1st century AD (possibly reworking a Maccabean-era text), writing as Moses' farewell to Joshua.
